interviewQuestions.question: Semantic vs instance segmentation — give a real product example of each.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd define the distinction first, then anchor it in products so it's concrete rather than textbook. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel by class but doesn't distinguish individual objects of the same class — a real example is an autonomous-driving perception stack labeling "drivable road surface" as one connected region; the car doesn't need to know it's looking at "road instance #1 and #2", it just needs to know which pixels are safely drivable. Instance segmentation separates individual object instances within the same class — a real example is a photo-editing app's "select subject" or background-blur feature (like portrait mode), where if there are three people in frame, the app needs to isolate each person as a distinct mask so you can, say, blur the background behind all three but keep each person individually editable. I'd close by noting the two aren't competing choices — they're suited to different questions, which is exactly why panoptic segmentation exists, to combine both into one unified output when a product genuinely needs both (e.g. "road" as semantic stuff plus "car #1", "car #2" as instances, in one self-driving frame).

**Testing:** whether you can map the abstract distinction onto concrete product decisions, not just recite the textbook definitions.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Grounding the distinction in real products

interviewQuestions.question: Why does U-Net need skip connections — what breaks if you remove them?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Without skip connections, U-Net degrades into a plain encoder-decoder: the encoder downsamples the image into a small, semantically rich bottleneck, and the decoder has to reconstruct a full-resolution, per-pixel output purely from that compressed representation. The problem is that downsampling is lossy in a very specific way — it destroys exactly the fine spatial detail (precise edges, thin structures, exact boundary location) needed to draw a crisp mask, while keeping the coarse "what object is this" information. The decoder can regenerate plausible-looking shapes from the bottleneck alone, but object boundaries come out blurry and imprecise because the information needed to place them exactly was thrown away several downsampling steps ago and can't be recovered from a compressed vector.

Skip connections fix this by copying the encoder's feature maps at each resolution directly across to the matching decoder stage, so the decoder gets both signals it needs at every scale: the coarse semantic context flowing up from the bottleneck, and the fine spatial detail arriving fresh from the same-resolution encoder stage, concatenated together before that decoder stage's convolutions run.

Concretely, this shows up most in thin or small structures — a blood vessel, a small lesion boundary — which is exactly why U-Net was invented for biomedical segmentation, where boundary precision on small structures is the entire point.

**Testing:** whether you understand skip connections as solving a specific information-loss problem, not just "a shape in the architecture diagram."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why skip connections matter

interviewQuestions.question: Your medical imaging model gets 95% pixel accuracy but the doctors say the masks are useless. What's wrong with the metric?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Pixel accuracy is dominated by whatever class covers the most pixels, and in medical imaging that's almost always background — a tumor or lesion is often a tiny fraction of the image. A model that predicts "background" everywhere and never finds the actual structure of interest can still score 95%+ pixel accuracy, because getting the huge background region right swamps getting the small, clinically important region completely wrong. That's exactly the class-imbalance trap pixel accuracy walks into, and it's why it's the wrong metric to report or optimize for here.

The fix is to use a metric that's sensitive to the small-object case specifically: the **Dice coefficient** (2 × overlap / sum of mask sizes) weights the overlap relative to both mask sizes rather than the whole image, so it penalizes missing a small structure far more heavily than pixel accuracy does — which is exactly why Dice is the standard in medical imaging. I'd also report **pixel-wise IoU** per class rather than an overall average, so a bad IoU on the minority class of interest can't hide behind a good overall number.

Beyond the metric, if training itself is struggling with the imbalance, I'd also check the loss function — plain per-pixel cross-entropy has the same imbalance problem as accuracy, and a Dice loss or a weighted loss that up-weights the rare class usually needs to replace it.

**Testing:** whether you connect a misleading metric to the class-imbalance root cause, and know the standard domain-appropriate fix (Dice) rather than just calling for "a better metric."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing a misleading segmentation metric
